Q: How to write a SELECT query with COUNT(), two JOINs, and GROUP BY in CodeIgniter A:
  • Chain your query builder method calls for maximum elegance.
  • Use all uppercase when writing SQL function names or keywords in builder method parameters. The exception is the third parameter of join() which will be rendered as all uppercase by CodeIgniter anyhow.
  • An INNER JOIN is synonymous with a plain JOIN, so there's no need to explicitly mention inner when calling join().
  • To avoid possible dialect/version errors, I generally advise to nominate all not aggregated columns in the group_by() call.
  • Pass the account id as a parameter into your model method.
  • Return an array of zero or more objects via result() or use result_array() if you want an array of zero or more arrays.
  • Like get(), get_where() executes the built query. This means that all other builder methods must be called earlier in the chain and the result() call must be last in the chain.
public function getDiscussionCountsPerPostForAccount(int $accountId): array
{
    return $this->db
        ->select('p._id, p.post_title, COUNT(d._id) total_discussions')
        ->join('discussions d', 'p._id = d.post_id')
        ->join('accounts a', 'a._id = p.account_id')
        ->group_by(['p._id', 'p.post_title'])
        ->get_where('posts p', ['a._id' => $accountId])
        ->result();
}

Call the model method from your controller like:

$postDiscussionCounts = $this->Posts_model->getDiscussionCountsPerPostForAccount('1494900911hRs5kjPXV9591a60afa434f');

Q: How to decode / view FCM push token? A:

It's not possible to decode the FCM token. The google intentionally prevents that.

Q: git: Is there a command line option for "Sort by date" for gitk? A:

The man gitk at least mentions it does take the same options than git rev-list, including

--date-order

This option is similar to --topo-order in the sense that no parent comes before all of its children, but otherwise things are still ordered in the commit timestamp order.

See "Guide to understanding gitk?" for more.

Note: if -d or --date-order is really the argument you are after, better not using too much, according to Linus himself (from lists-archives.com/git or www.spinics.net/lists/git/):

The thing is, --date-order strings out and mixes up the commits on the same development chain, and by doing so it makes the different chains of development much harder to see.
It also ends up showing the development in a more "parallel" way, which in turn makes the view even harder to read.

So I would suggest not using --date-order by default. It doesn't add anything to any normal flow, and it makes the big picture harder to see.

The only time you really want --date-order (or "-d", which is shorthand for it for just gitk) is really

  • when the big picture is really really simple, and you actually want to see more detail because the big picture is too trivial to even be interesting otherwise.
    (In other words: --date-order is fine for really simple development where there is only ever just a couple of branches or where you have pruned away so much of the history that the remaining part is simple)
  • when you want to debug "git rev-list" behaviour itself, since the date order actually matters for how git traverses the commit chains.

The second case is something that I suspect nobody but me and a few other people have ever done.
I found it very useful together with --show-all when I was debugging the revision walker (see commits "Add "--show-all" revision walker flag for debugging" and "Make revision limiting more robust against occasional bad commit dates ", where the first implements --show-all, and the second one is the end result of my debugging).

In other words: never start out with "-d" or "--date-order" by default.
Only if you have some reason to then think that the view is too simple or you need to drill down into the commit relationships should you use it.

As noted by huancz in the comments, if your workflow is essentially:

  • feature branches get rebased onto dev,
  • dev gets merged into main,
  • and main is mostly (or only) merge commits,

then gitk --all can indeed become a spaghetti bowl of long-lived colored lines leading into old, now-irrelevant side history.
In that scenario, date order can be a better "default mental model", because you are often asking:

"what happened recently / what merges landed, in time order?"

rather than

"what is the cleanest topological picture?"

Since "always --all --date-order" is not readily available as a global config option, you might consider instead:

  • Focus on the branch you care about (often enough):

    gitk main

  • If main is merge-driven, consider keeping only the first-parent chain (this collapses away most side-history noise while preserving a sensible story of what landed on main):

    gitk main --first-parent

    You can still add --date-order if you prefer that presentation.

  • If you still want "everything" but less clutter, try limiting by time (rev-list style), using gitk --since:

    gitk --all --since="2 weeks ago"

    That keeps the graph relevant without permanently changing ordering

I want date-order. I came here while searching how to MAKE it a default. Guess alias is still the only way.

True, an alias/wrapper is usually the simplest

  • Shell alias (bash/zsh):

    alias gitk='gitk --date-order'

  • Git alias (so you can run git k ...):

    git config --global alias.k '!gitk --date-order "$@"'
# then: git k --all

That way, people who benefit from --date-order (your "merge-only main" style) can make it the default for them, while still keeping the topo-order view available when they need the structural picture.

Q: Does TOML support top level arrays of dictionaries? A:

TOML does not permit a top level array.

From github.com/toml-lang/toml:

TOML always has a hash table at the top level of the file, which can easily have data nested inside its keys, but it doesn't permit top-level arrays or floats, so it cannot directly serialize some data.
